summary:
The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all sexual activity outside heterosexual marriage. Articles 233 to 239 define the offences in anatomical terms and set 100 lashes for the receptive partner in sodomy, 100 lashes for intercrural sex, 31 to 74 lashes for other intimate acts between men, and 100 lashes for tribadism with death on a fourth conviction. The code does not distinguish consensual from non-consensual conduct, and NGOs report that in assault cases both victim and perpetrator are held criminally liable.

The UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the legal framework carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes.

Transgender identity is legally recognised only through sex reassignment surgery. Under Article 20, Clause 14 a person who has had surgery may change name and gender on the birth certificate by court order; the CPIN states that recognition follows surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process, and that an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

The state funds gender-reassignment surgery. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans of up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for the procedure, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover it. Reporting in 2024 and 2025 describes the same policy as coercive: foreign patients travel for state-subsidised surgery while Iranian trans people face pressure to complete a binary transition or face legal penalty for living outside it.

Identity documents can expose holders. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that the disclosure identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination.

Authorities have restricted trans people's presence in public space. Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas, an official advisory limiting where trans residents may be seen.

Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility in an open letter published by HRANA. 6Rang has documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct.

The enforcement backdrop includes executions and mass arrests. Human Rights Watch recorded two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005; records show at least 107 executions on charges related to homosexuality between 1979 and 1990, a raw count over an eleven-year period with no per-capita denominator supplied. Police in Isfahan raided a party in February 2008 and arrested 30 men held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity, and an April 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province led to 30 arrests, with detainees taken to Dastgerd Prison and told they would be executed. The most recent documented killing in this record is the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared, allegedly by relatives; no later killing is documented here.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognised, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex has no standing recognition of that partnership.

Social treatment differs by direction of transition. Trans men are more visible socially and find acceptance more easily than trans women, who are often misgendered and placed in the same category as gay men.

No legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Security forces have harassed, arrested and detained individuals suspected of being gay or transgender, raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and those accused of sodomy often face summary trials.
tangentialFactors:
Displacement is documented as a response to the legal regime. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (February 2025), 'They See Us as Criminals', surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who had fled Iran, 96 per cent of them from ethnic minorities, and recorded systematic persecution as the driver of their departure. A 6Rang submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review (48th session, January-February 2025) separately documented human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

Religious authority on reassignment is split. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei legally recognises reassignment, while Grand Ayatollah Yousef Madani Tabrizi has called it unlawful, and several senior clerics hold that reassignment is not permissible for cross-dressers or people engaging in same-sex behaviour.

Judicial outcomes vary in severity. In 2022 two gay men in Maragheh received death sentences for 'sodomy by force', a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy; the sentences were later commuted to life in prison. The legal code sets the death penalty at 18 for adults and at 15 for murder, and a 2017 US State Department report raised concerns about LGBTI minors.

Exit routes are documented. Iranian transgender people who flee to Türkiye seek UNHCR asylum, and since October 2008 the Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees has provided basic necessities, financial aid and private sponsorship for resettlement in Canada, with prolonged waiting periods. The raw execution count of at least 107 cases between 1979 and 1990 is a count only; no population or per-capita figure accompanies it, so it cannot be used to rank risk against other jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Legal recognition of a gender change requires sex reassignment surgery and a court order under Article 20, Clause 14 of the civil code. Petitioners also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a 'rational benefit', with medical approval required to establish dissonance between assigned gender and experienced gender. Corrected identity documents have reportedly been issued efficiently and transparently.

The legal-religious basis traces to a 1964 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini approving surgery while in exile, a 1983 fatwa allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation; practice has been legal since the mid-1980s under medical approval and is partially financially supported by the state. A 1976 Iranian Medical Association ruling held such surgeries unethical except for intersex individuals.

Some homosexual individuals have been pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a route to conformity. Enforcement has been stricter against gay men than lesbians.

Since the mid-2000s the government has provided grants of up to 45 million rials and loans of up to 55 million rials for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover the procedure. HIV/AIDS medication is free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist. Homosexuals, bisexuals and lesbians are banned from donating blood.

The government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, so that role has fallen to exiled groups including the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran. Traditional families exercise strong influence over marriage and dating, few LGBTQ Iranians come out to family, and gay couples report fear of being seen together in public.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory supplies no date for the Tehran advisory restricting transgender people's presence in busy areas, and none for the open letter by Ghazal Marzban recounting rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility; both are recorded here as undated in this record.

No material in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules, airport or border screening of gender presentation, identity-document checks at the frontier, or access to gender-appropriate facilities. Nothing here should be read as an assessment of those points.

No hate-crime provision covering gender identity or sexual orientation is sourced, and the absence of anti-discrimination legislation is stated by the sources rather than inferred. Whether any non-legislative protection mechanism exists is not sourced.

Third-country asylum outcomes recorded in the inventory (Netherlands, United Kingdom, Japan, Sweden, UNHCR decisions between 2001 and 2006) concern other jurisdictions' policies and are not assessed here.

The execution figure of at least 107 cases between 1979 and 1990 is a raw count with no denominator, and no current homicide or violence rate for trans people in Iran is available in this inventory, so no comparative risk magnitude can be stated.
